questions.q: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the beginning of a singly linked list, and why does it not depend on the list length?
questions.a: O(1) — insertion at head only requires creating a new node, pointing its `next` to the current head, and updating the head reference. No traversal is needed. A wrong answer like O(n) reveals the student thinks traversal is always required, confusing head insertion with position-based insertion.

questions.q: In a singly linked list with nodes A → B → C, you want to insert node X between A and B. Explain why you must modify A's `next` pointer *before* modifying X's `next` pointer, and what goes wrong if you reverse the order.
questions.a: If you set X.next = A.next first, X points to B. Then setting A.next = X completes the chain A → X → B. If you reverse: A.next = X makes A point to X, but X.next still points to N/A (or garbage), so B and the rest of the list become unreachable — memory leak and data loss. A wrong answer shows the student doesn't understand pointer dependency order.

questions.q: Write Python code to delete the node at position 3 (1-indexed) in a singly linked list. Handle the case where the list has fewer than 3 nodes.
Compare the pointer changes when deleting the *last* node versus deleting the *first* node in a singly linked list of length ≥ 2. Why is tail deletion O(n) while head deletion is O(1)?
questions.a: Head deletion: only `head = head.next` — constant time. Tail deletion: must traverse to the second-last node (position n-1) to set its `next = N/A`, requiring O(n) steps. The asymmetry exists because singly linked lists only have forward pointers — no direct access to the predecessor of the tail. A wrong answer claiming both are O(1) shows the student assumes a `tail` pointer exists or that backward traversal is possible.

questions.q:
A student writes this insertion-at-position code:
```python
def insert_at_pos(head, data, pos):
    new_node = Node(data)
    if pos == 1:
        new_node.next = head
        return new_node
    curr = head
    for _ in range(pos - 1):
        curr = curr.next
    new_node.next = curr.next
    curr.next = new_node
    return head
```
Identify two distinct bugs in this code and explain the scenario each bug breaks.
questions.a: Bug 1: Loop runs `pos-1` times instead of `pos-2` — moves `curr` to the *target position* instead of the *node before it*. Breaks when inserting at position 2: `curr` becomes the old head, then `curr.next = new_node` creates a cycle. Bug 2: No check for `curr is N/A` inside the loop — if `pos > length+1`, `curr` becomes `N/A` and `curr.next` raises AttributeError. A student missing both bugs hasn't traced pointer positions carefully.

questions.q: Design a singly linked list operation `insert_sorted(head, data)` that inserts a new node with `data` into a list *already sorted in ascending order* so the list remains sorted. Describe the algorithm in 4-5 steps and state its time complexity.
questions.a: Steps: (1) Create new_node. (2) If head is N/A or data ≤ head.data, insert at head and return new_node. (3) Traverse with `curr = head` while `curr.next` exists and `curr.next.data < data`, moving `curr = curr.next`. (4) Insert: `new_node.next = curr.next; curr.next = new_node`. (5) Return head. Time complexity: O(n) worst case (insert at end), O(1) best case (insert at head). A poor answer that suggests sorting the whole list after insertion reveals the student doesn't leverage the pre-sorted property.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Linked List insertion and deletion are ______ dynamic memory operations that modify the structure of a singly linked list by adding new nodes or removing existing nodes while maintaining the sequential chain of references.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're building a music ______ manager where songs can be added or removed anywhere — not just at the ends like a stack or queue.
What is Linked List insertion and deletion? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Linked List insertion and deletion are fundamental dynamic memory operations that modify the structure of a singly linked list by adding new nodes or removing existing nodes while maintaining the sequential chain of references.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Linked List insertion and deletion?
questions.a: Students believe that "deleting a node" in Python means explicitly calling del node or node = N/A to free memory.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to trace pointer changes step-by-step for insertion/deletion at head, tail, and arbitrary positions in a singly linked list, write correct Python code for all six cases (insert at beginning/end/position, delete from beginning/end/position), and explain the time complexity (O(1) for head operations, O(n) for.
